qa_pair.question: A team must sort a list of 1,024 records, and their only hard guarantee is that the algorithm's running time never exceeds a constant multiple of $n \log_2 n$ comparisons for *any* input ordering, including the worst one. Among the classic comparison-based sorts, merge sort is the standard choice because its worst-case running time is ____.
qa_pair.explanation: Merge sort always splits the array into two halves (about $\log_2 n$ levels of recursion) and each level does linear work to merge, giving $\Theta(n \log n)$ comparisons regardless of the input order. Unlike quick sort, whose worst case degrades to $O(n^2)$ on already-sorted or badly pivoted input, merge sort's worst case is the same as its average case: $O(n \log n)$. For $n = 1024$ that is roughly $1024 \times 10 = 10{,}240$ comparisons at each level's total, i.e. on the order of $n \log n$ work overall.
